co_upper_satellite_boulders.blurb: Upper Satellite Boulders is a quieter pocket of Flatirons bouldering above Boulder, a stiff hike beyond the busier Satellite group. The blocks collect in a drainage under the Second Flatiron, with more piled into a scree slope reaching toward the Third. Expect tall free-standing boulders and leaning slabs that make short, steep lines. Of the 21 problems, a handful are easy, most land between V4 and V9, and one outlier is far harder at V12. Sitting several hundred feet higher than the lower boulders, it stays cooler in summer, while winter sun is scarce and snow lingers. Few people make the trip, so it suits a climber wanting space.

co_sesame_street.blurb: Sesame Street is a high-elevation sport crag above Telluride, reached by trail up the Bear Creek canyon at roughly 10,500 feet. The conglomerate cliff faces east, so it catches early sun and slips into shade later in the day. Its 21 sport routes lean hard: fifteen sit in the 5.12 to 5.13 range, four are 5.10, and the rest fill in between. That makes it one of the better places near town for climbers working at a high level, with fewer options for those who want an easy warm-up. Expect a sizeable uphill hike before you tie in.

co_10_2150_wall.blurb: 2150 Wall is one of the north-side walls at The Bank on Shelf Road, outside Canon City. It is a smooth, clean panel of limestone split by a crack, and it is the most noticeable wall in view from the lot. Nearly all of the 21 climbs are bolted: a few moderates at the left end, plenty of 5.9 and 5.10 lines, and the strongest showing in the 5.11 range, with a few 5.12s above that. Facing southwest, it takes sun for most of the afternoon with little shade, so it suits cool days. Expect company, since this part of the canyon is popular.
co_10_2150_wall.approach: Walk down the dirt road into The Bank, take the clear trail on the right, drop into the wash, cross it and climb the far side. Follow the signs toward the wall; the trail meets its middle section.

co_boulder_city.blurb: Boulder City is a bouldering zone in the San Luis Valley, part of the Alamosa Canyon area that locals also call Heavy Metal, at around 8,700 feet. A cliff band and a scatter of free-standing boulders stretch along roughly three miles, and some call it the densest cluster of loose blocks in the valley. Of the 21 problems here, most fall between V3 and V7, with a few harder ones reaching V11 and one easy option. The rock is sharp and can be chossy, and afternoons run hot, so mornings or cooler days work best. It feels remote and rough rather than polished.

co_southeast_face_2.blurb: The Southeast Face is the main multi-pitch wall on Greyrock, a granite peak northwest of Fort Collins in the Poudre Canyon area. It is a slabby face laced with cracks, giving long moderate trad lines of up to about five pitches and roughly 500 feet. Almost all of the 21 routes are trad, with most between 5.6 and 5.9 and just a few reaching 5.10 or 5.11. The left portion mixes ledges with slabs and faces, while the right is more sustained. Summer thunderstorms are a real consideration, so start early. It rewards climbers who enjoy long, easier days over short hard ones.
co_southeast_face_2.approach: Follow the Summit trail until it runs along the base of the wall, then leave it and scramble uphill in the forest until you reach the face.

co_horseshead.blurb: Horseshead is a steep pyramid of rock, about 250 feet tall, on the west flank of Palisade Mountain in the Big Thompson Canyon area near Estes Park. It holds 21 routes, all trad, running from easy 5.6 to 5.12. The grade spread is centered on the 5.10s, with a good handful at 5.8 and 5.11 too, and several climbs run longer than one pitch. There is no real trail in, so reaching the base takes route-finding across a plateau, a draw and a steep gully; it is a committing outing rather than a quick crag day. The reward is wide views over the Front Range.

co_shirt_tail_peak.blurb: Shirt Tail Peak crowns the Redgarden Wall side of Eldorado Canyon State Park near Boulder and is the highest point in the park. Its 21 routes are all trad, from easy 5.5 up to 5.12, with the heart of the range in the 5.8 to 5.11 band. Many are multi-pitch lines up serrated aretes and faces, and ledges hold loose rock, so move with care. It sees far fewer people than the famous walls below, and the summit gives big views toward the Flatirons and Indian Peaks. The southwest side bakes in afternoon sun, so an early start helps. Expect a steep, loose walk to reach the base.
